title: Mass intentions
hook: a Mass can be offered for someone living or dead; any offering is a gift, not a price

segments.voice: Yesterday, requiem: the old prayer of rest and light for the dead. Your line was let perpetual light shine. Whose name came to you, and did it get its moment? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

The back page of a parish bulletin, under the Mass times. Saturday evening: for Maria Lopez, deceased. Sunday morning: for the Kowalski family. Tuesday: in thanksgiving, for a safe surgery. Wednesday: for a grandmother, on her birthday. Then, on Saturday evening, the priest says it aloud near the start or in the prayers: this Mass is offered for Maria. A few people in the pews look up. One of them is the one who asked. What does it mean to say a Mass is for someone? And what about the envelope that went to the parish office? Today, Mass intentions.
screen: `THE BACK PAGE OF THE BULLETIN.` → `THIS MASS IS OFFERED FOR MARIA.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE ENVELOPE?`

segments.voice: Start with the old root of the custom. In the second book of Maccabees, after a battle, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection and sends the silver to Jerusalem so that a sacrifice can be offered for the soldiers who had died. That's the passage that closed with yesterday's holy and wholesome thought. Catholics see in it the shape of a Mass intention: an offering, a sacrifice, and a particular person held up to God. Next, who a Mass can be for. Anyone. The living and the dead. A sick friend, a newborn, a marriage on its anniversary, a soldier far away. Church law says a priest is free to apply the Mass for anyone, living or dead. It doesn't have to be a Catholic. Then the envelope. Church law allows a priest to accept an offering from someone who asks for a Mass for their intention. But the same law insists there must be no hint of trade or commerce in it. The offering is a gift that supports the Church and its priests, not a price that buys a Mass. The law even urges priests to celebrate Mass for the intentions of the faithful, especially the poor, without receiving any offering at all. If you can't give, you can still ask. Last, what the intention does and doesn't do. The Saturday evening Mass isn't a different Mass, and Maria isn't the only person it touches. The whole Church prays, and Christ's offering is the same. The intention simply names one face inside it, the way you might hold up one photograph in a crowded room and say, especially her.
screen: `A COLLECTION SENT TO JERUSALEM.` · `FOR ANYONE, LIVING OR DEAD.` · `A GIFT, NOT A PRICE.` · `ONE FACE INSIDE THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `THIS MASS IS OFFERED FOR...`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to request a Mass for someone. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself who comes to mind first. Someone who has died, someone sick, someone starting something new, someone you're worried about and can't help. Let one person settle. Hold their face, and simply wish them every good thing for one long breath. If you're Catholic, or would like to be part of this, you can plan to call a parish office this week and ask for a Mass for them. If not, keep them close for the rest of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mass intentions. Asking a priest to offer a Mass for a particular person, living or dead, often with an offering given as a gift, never as a price. Today's word.

Your line: a mass for them. Today, look up a parish office number and ask for a Mass for someone, or simply write that person's name somewhere you'll see it tonight. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Catholics ask a parish to have a Mass offered for a living or deceased person, usually through the parish office, and the intention is often listed in the bulletin or mentioned at that Mass. Some give an offering when they ask; Church law forbids any appearance of buying the Mass and urges priests to accept intentions from the poor without one.

original.note: Latin, the application of the Mass: the Church's term for offering a Mass for a particular intention.

trapdoor: what you thought: you pay the parish and a Mass gets said for your person.
what it means: you ask a priest to offer a Mass for someone, living or dead; any offering is a gift that supports the Church.
what a scholar hears: canon law lets a priest apply the Mass for anyone, excludes all appearance of trade in Mass offerings, and urges Masses for the poor even without one.

notes: Canon 901 paraphrased: a priest is free to apply the Mass for anyone, living or dead. Canon 945 §1–2: a priest may receive an offering to apply the Mass for a specific intention; priests are earnestly recommended to celebrate Mass for the intentions of the faithful, especially the needy, even without receiving an offering. Canon 947: any appearance of trafficking or trading is to be entirely excluded from Mass offerings. Confirm paraphrases.
2 Maccabees 12:43 paraphrased (Judas takes up a collection and sends silver to Jerusalem for a sacrifice for the dead); the amount in the text is omitted on purpose.
Bulletin names in the hook are invented examples, not real people;

'The intention names one face inside it' is an image, not a doctrinal formula; a Keeper may want to add the distinction between the general fruits of the Mass and the special fruit applied to the intention, or keep it simple.
